meta.description: How Charles-Erick BG made a legacy marketing SaaS platform simpler for experts and newcomers alike: data import, navigation, dashboards and design system.

glance.v: A legacy platform that was hard to learn, costly to support and slow to evolve, used by long-time experts and newcomers alike.
User research, product design, information architecture, design system
Customers *much easier to onboard* according to the CSMs, key features *praised by in-house experts*, and *almost no support requests* when the menu was completely overhauled.

sections.caption: The campaign dashboard, one of the four pillars. I recreated the visuals to respect the non-disclosure agreement.
sections.lead: At Market Inc., I helped put a legacy marketing SaaS platform, complex and hard to get started with, *on the path to a world-class SaaS* that can compete with the likes of Adobe. Of all my projects, four were the pillars, from research to launch: data import, main navigation, statistics dashboards and the design system. One thread ties them together: serve the experts without discouraging the newcomers.

items.note: Market Inc. is a pseudonym; the client is protected by a non-disclosure agreement.

sections.label: The friction
sections.h2: A platform that was *hard to learn and slow to evolve*
sections.lead: Long-time customers who knew every screen worked alongside newcomers, some of them uneasy with technology, and developer-minded users. Every redesign had to serve both ends.

items.p: The main menu held almost every feature, actions included. New users didn’t know where to go.
Scattered paths (the API in one place, files in another), options hidden in an “advanced” interface, and errors with no explanation.
Each channel had its own statistics, with no shared foundation. [À FOURNIR : to validate]
With no design system tied to the code, developers rebuilt components that were hard to maintain afterwards.

sections.label: The cost to the business
sections.h2: Time lost *in support, onboarding and development*

items.p: The learning curve was steep: users had to ask internal teams many questions before they could use the platform.
Without clear errors, debugging an import often went through support and the CSMs.
Adding a channel meant designing its screens from scratch. [À FOURNIR : to validate]
Legacy ASPX pages with an old design system lived alongside the new technology, which forced trade-offs.
Bring every import into a single step-by-step flow that explains the platform as you use it.
Pick up a redesign started by others and carry it through to retiring the old menu.
Create a reusable campaign statistics template for every channel.
Bring in Figma, structure the design system and tie it to the developers’ Storybook.

items.h: Bring imports into one flow that teaches the platform
items.p: A single entry point, moved from the main menu to the Contacts section, then five steps: *what to import, how, settings, field mapping and analysis*. The cards on the first screen explain each type of data: users learn how the platform is structured while importing.

list: One screen that handles every import the same way.

list.t: A step-by-step flow that adapts to what you import.

notes.v: New users got lost, and unexplained errors filled the support queue. I added a preview of the file’s first rows so people could map fields without opening it on the side, and, with the developers, errors that say what to fix, where and how.
Users of the old import had to relearn. For them, the old options stayed in the flow, and settings hidden in the “advanced” interface became available to everyone.

items.h: Measure every step and fix fast, in small increments
items.p: After launch, I set up *a step-by-step funnel in Microsoft Clarity*. It showed many drop-offs on the very first screen: people landed there looking for something else.

list: Fix it later, in a future redesign.

list.t: Fix it right away, with a small improvement.

notes.v: Adding information links to the first screen, an idea borrowed from the market’s biggest players, was a small, quick and inexpensive change. More people then moved on to the next step. [À FOURNIR : funnel figures, if available]
A slightly busier first screen. In return, the team had a continuous optimization loop: measure, form a hypothesis, ship small, measure again.

items.h: Organize the menu by use case: think like a marketer, not a developer
items.p: The main menu now holds *only sections, each built around a need*: browse contacts, launch a campaign, acquire customers, automate. Actions live in section headers, and import becomes a button in Contacts.

list: A menu organized around how the system works, with actions as destinations.

list.t: A menu organized around what marketers need, with actions in context.

notes.v: The best in the industry keep navigation light: you enter a context, and that’s where you find the options. I validated the architecture in Miro with every internal team until the founders bought in, then through weekly task-based tests.
We had to prioritize which pages to modernize and accept interim solutions that led to legacy pages (see the challenge below).

shots.label: [À FOURNIR] New menu and section header

items.h: Launch alongside the old version to reduce risk
items.p: For several months, *customers could switch between the old and the new menu*. In-app announcements asked for their feedback, and the CSMs gave them plenty of notice.

list: Replace the old menu all at once.

list.t: Replace the old menu gradually, with both side by side.

notes.v: The customer base was expert, set in its habits and demanding. More than 25 customer interviews, run with the marketing team, shaped the message of the banners, modals and display rules.
Maintaining two menus for several months. When the old one was retired, customers already knew the new one, and support received almost no requests.

items.h: One dashboard template for every channel
items.p: Rather than designing each channel’s statistics separately, I created *a reusable template* that covers about 99% of a new channel such as WhatsApp or RCS.

list: A custom dashboard for each channel.

notes.v: I reviewed every dashboard in the platform and those of the biggest players in the market to spot the patterns that recur by sending channel. A shared template makes each new channel faster to ship and consistent with the others.
Each channel keeps its specifics: for an RCS carousel, clicks appear in two tables, one for RCS and one for the fallback SMS.

items.h: Tie Figma to Storybook so design and code speak the same language
items.p: I led *the move from Adobe XD to Figma* across the company, then structured the design system with the team: documented sections, configurable components, and a growing link to the developers’ Storybook.

list: Stay on Adobe XD, with components rebuilt in code as needed.

list.t: Move to Figma, with components tied to the code in Storybook.

notes.v: Ship faster, without developers reinventing components that are hard to maintain. I convinced leadership, justified the costs through to purchase, managed licences and archived the old mockups.
A migration to run alongside ongoing projects. The navigation’s action headers and the dashboard template were its first applications.

sections.label: An unexpected design challenge
prose: The new navigation ran on recent technology, but several pages were still in ASPX, with an old design system and an old look. The two didn’t always work well together.
**Redoing everything at once was impossible.** So I set out an overall plan, even without every answer, and prioritized the pages to modernize with the product team.
For pages not yet redesigned, I designed *interim solutions*: for example, an empty state in a new page with a button to the legacy page, until that page was redesigned and became the real one.

sections.label: The system
sections.lead: An info icon explains each metric, a flame icon flags results above the industry benchmark, and a purple card puts the return on investment front and centre.

sections.label: What users said
sections.lead: Both ends adopted the new screens: power users prefer them, and the CSMs onboard new customers more easily.

items.p: According to the CSMs, onboarding new customers has been much easier since the new import, a key and frequently used step of onboarding.
Thanks to the gradual transition, retiring the old menu generated practically no requests.

items.h: A platform that is easier to sell
items.p: The sales team noted that the platform had become much easier to sell, a collective result of the product team.
